title: Plugins and ServiceLoader
idea: A plugin architecture lets you add features as new classes behind a stable interface, discovered at startup, without editing the host code.
points: The host owns a small interface, the extension point; plugins only implement it.
A registry maps each plugin to a key and rejects duplicates loudly.
`ServiceLoader` finds implementations listed in `META-INF/services` files on the class path.
Discovery order is not a contract: sort plugins, or give them an explicit priority.

edges.label: load
edges.caption: The host asks `ServiceLoader` for every `Codec`. It names no concrete class.

edges.label: read
edges.caption: The loader reads each `META-INF/services` file named after the interface on the class path.

edges.label: ships
edges.caption: A plugin jar ships that file listing its implementation classes. Adding the jar adds the plugin.

edges.label: instantiate
edges.caption: For each listed name the loader loads the class and calls its public no-arg constructor.

edges.label: implements
edges.caption: Each plugin implements the interface, so the dependency points from plugin to host.

edges.label: Codec list
edges.caption: The host receives instances typed as `Codec`, sorts them, and uses them like any object.

code.title: An explicit plugin registry
code.caption: The host knows only `Exporter`. A new format is a new class plus one `register` call.

walk.text: The extension point: a key and one operation. Keep it small so plugins stay easy to write.
`putIfAbsent` registers once; a second plugin claiming the same key fails at startup.
An unknown key fails with a message that lists what is available.
A `TreeMap` gives a stable, sorted order for listing and for printing.
Adding JSON needed no change to the registry: the Open/Closed Principle (OCP) in practice.
Each plugin is a small `final` class with no knowledge of the others.

code.title: Discovery with ServiceLoader
code.caption: With no services file nothing is found. Writing the file, as a plugin jar would, makes both plugins appear.

walk.text: `ServiceLoader.load` returns lazy providers; `get` creates each instance when asked.
Sort by name: the order files are found in is not guaranteed.
The services file is named after the interface and lists one provider class per line.
Temp files are deleted at exit. A child class loader over the folder stands in for a jar.
Providers must be public with a public no-arg constructor.
The services file needs binary names: a nested class is `Outer$Inner`.
The host code is identical in both calls. Try-with-resources closes each class loader.

pitfalls: Giving a provider only a constructor with arguments: `ServiceLoader` fails with a `ServiceConfigurationError`.
Relying on discovery order: two jars on a different class path can swap which plugin wins.
Letting plugins reach into host internals: every host refactor then breaks third-party plugins.

quiz.q: A team adds a new `Codec` jar, but `ServiceLoader` does not find it. What is the most likely cause?
options: No services file named after the `Codec` interface
`ServiceLoader` only finds classes in the host's own jar
quiz.why: Without a module descriptor, `ServiceLoader` discovers providers only through `META-INF/services/<interface name>` files on the class path. No file, no provider.

takeaway: Own the interface, let plugins implement it, and register them by key.

starters: How does `provides ... with` in module-info replace the services file?
